title: Winn v. Brady
description: Whether a recorded judgment lien constitutes a constitutionally protected property interest, entitling junior lienholders to personal notice of an execution sale, and whether this rule should apply retroactively or prospectively.
plaintiff_argument: Junior judgment lienholders hold a constitutionally protected property interest and are entitled to personal notice of an execution sale, not merely notice by publication, to satisfy due process.
defendant_argument: The execution sale was not a state action, thus due process rights were not implicated, and they complied with statutory notice requirements by publication.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that junior judgment lienholders are entitled to personal notice consistent with due process, but reversed the Intermediate Court of Appeals' decision to apply this rule to the instant case, holding that the new rule shall apply prospectively only.

title: Hawaii v. Zuffante
description: Whether the Hawaiʻi Constitution's due process clause requires law enforcement to record custodial interrogations, both in-station and, when feasible, outside the station, with the plaintiff arguing against such a requirement and the defendant arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Hawaiʻi argued that existing precedent (Kekona) did not require recording and that current times did not warrant overturning that rule.
defendant_argument: Charles Zuffante argued that the lack of recording undermined his right against self-incrimination and a fair trial, urging the court to adopt a recording requirement.
decision_outcome: The court held that the Hawaiʻi Constitution's due process clause requires law enforcement to record all in-station custodial interrogations and, when feasible, all outside-the-station custodial interrogations, overruling State v. Kekona. The lower court's judgment and sentence against Zuffante were vacated, and the case was remanded.

title: Grube v. Trader; State v. Rogan
description: Whether the circuit court erred in sealing judicial records related to a criminal proceeding and in requiring a reporter to retain counsel to assert his constitutional right of public access to those records.
plaintiff_argument: Grube argued that the circuit court failed to meet the procedural and substantive requirements for sealing records, and that he had a personal constitutional right to represent himself pro se in asserting public access to judicial records.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the circuit court properly identified a compelling interest in preserving ongoing investigations, that the sealing order was narrowly tailored, and that Grube, as a non-attorney, could not represent Civil Beat's interests.
decision_outcome: The court granted Grube's petition for a writ of mandamus, ordering the circuit court to unseal the documents (unless the State requests a hearing to provide additional evidence within ten days) and permitting Grube to represent himself pro se in further proceedings. The court denied the writ of prohibition as unnecessary.

title: Hilo Bay Marina v. State of Hawaii
description: Whether a state deed restriction requiring land use for "church purposes only" violates the Hawaiʻi Constitution's Establishment Clause, with the plaintiff arguing it constitutes state action advancing religion and the defendant arguing for alignment with federal First Amendment interpretations allowing more religious accommodation.
plaintiff_argument: The deed restriction requiring land use for "church purposes only" constitutes state action that advances religion and violates Hawaiʻi’s Establishment Clause, which mandates a strict separation of church and state.
defendant_argument: The Hawaiʻi Constitution's Establishment Clause should be interpreted co-extensively with the federal First Amendment, and recent U.S. Supreme Court rulings (like Kennedy) allow for greater accommodation of religion, making the deed restriction permissible.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Circuit Court erred in granting summary judgment to the State and that summary judgment is warranted for Hilo Bay, indicating the deed restriction is a violation of the Establishment Clause.

title: Foresman v. Foresman
description: Whether HRS § 657-1.8(a) violates the ex post facto clause of the U.S. Constitution and whether the Circuit Court should have instructed the jury on criminal statutes in effect at the time of the alleged sexual abuse rather than when the complaint was filed.
plaintiff_argument: HRS § 657-1.8 is constitutional, and any error in jury instructions was harmless because the defendant's admitted conduct would have constituted a criminal offense under statutes in effect at the time of the acts.
defendant_argument: HRS § 657-1.8(a) is unconstitutional as it violates the ex post facto clause by imposing civil liability for acts not criminal when committed, and the Circuit Court erred by using subsequently enacted criminal statutes for jury instructions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Intermediate Court of Appeals' judgment, which upheld the Circuit Court's final judgment, finding that while the jury instructions were erroneous, the error was harmless given the defendant's admissions.

title: State v. Hoffman
description: Whether a defendant's un-Mirandized statements made in response to a police officer's words "normally attendant to arrest and custody" are admissible, or if such statements constitute "interrogation" under the Hawaiʻi State Constitution if they were reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response, thereby requiring Miranda warnings.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Hoffman's statements were made in response to Officer Tavares's statements or actions "normally attendant to arrest and custody" and therefore did not constitute "interrogation," and that the ICA erred in suppressing certain statements.
defendant_argument: Hoffman argued that the ICA gravely erred by ruling that an officer's conduct and statements "normally attendant to arrest and custody" could not amount to an interrogation triggering Miranda warnings, asserting that such statements are still subject to the inquiry of whether they were reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and vacated in part the ICA's judgment, and vacated in part the circuit court's order, holding that some of Hoffman's statements were made in response to interrogation and should be suppressed, while others were not and are admissible.

title: Surface Water Use Permit Applications
description: Whether the Commission on Water Resource Management (CWRM) properly determined surface water use permits and interim instream flow standards for Nā Wai 'Ehā, or if its decisions violated constitutional and statutory mandates, due process rights, and unlawfully delegated authority.
plaintiff_argument: The various appellants (MMK, Hui/MTF, OHA, Mahi Pono, WWC) argue that the CWRM's decision failed to restore stream flows to the extent practicable, unlawfully delegated public trust duties, made erroneous water allocations, and violated due process rights.
defendant_argument: The Commission on Water Resource Management (CWRM) maintains that it properly decided water allocations and instream flow standards, complied with its mandates, and did not violate due process or unlawfully delegate authority.
decision_outcome: The court vacated and remanded the Commission's decision regarding interim instream flow standards, the unlawful delegation of public trust duties, and the lack of clarity in Mahi Pono's water allocation, while affirming the Commission's decisions on MMK's water allocation, MMK's 12-MAV monitoring, WWC's due process claims, WWC's PUC jurisdiction argument, and other conditions attached to WWC's permit.

title: State v. Tran
description: Whether Hawai'i's statute regarding continuous sexual assault of a minor and a related constitutional provision violate the U.S. Constitution's Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments by allowing nonunanimous jury verdicts on specific predicate acts, and whether the indictment against Alvin Tran was sufficiently specific.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Hawai'i constitutional provision and statute do not violate the U.S. Constitution because they do not authorize nonunanimous jury verdicts, and that Ramos did not require unanimity on specific predicate acts. The State also argued the indictment was sufficient under the liberal construction standard.
defendant_argument: Tran argued that the Hawai'i constitutional provision and statute violate the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments by allowing nonunanimous juries to convict without agreement on specific predicate acts, and that the indictment was insufficiently specific under Jardine.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the circuit court's order granting in part and denying in part Tran's motion to dismiss, affirmed the circuit court's denial of Tran's supplemented new trial motion, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Kanahele v. State
description: Whether Act 14 of 1995 precludes claims regarding the 2018 designation of the Mauna Kea Access Road (MKAR) as a state highway, with plaintiffs arguing it does not and defendants arguing it does.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Act 14 of 1995 does not bar their claims because the 2018 designation of the MKAR as a state highway constituted a new breach of trust, and the State failed to follow proper procedures for this designation, violating its fiduciary duties under the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act (HHCA).
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Act 14 of 1995 fully and finally resolved all claims related to the uncompensated use of Hawaiian home lands for state roads and highways, including the MKAR, and the 2018 designation did not give rise to any new claims.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the circuit court's summary judgment in favor of the defendants and remanded the case with instructions to grant summary judgment to the plaintiffs.

title: Davis v. Bissen
description: Whether constitutional due process required a contested case hearing before the County of Maui could remove houseless plaintiffs and their belongings from County property.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that they possessed a constitutionally protected property interest in their chattels and that due process required a contested case hearing before the County could seize and destroy their property.
defendant_argument: The County argued that the plaintiffs did not have a constitutionally protected property interest in storing their chattels on public land, or that if they did, alternative procedures provided sufficient due process without a contested case hearing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's denial of the County's motion to dismiss as to plaintiffs Davis and Lau, holding that constitutional due process required a pre-deprivation contested case hearing for their seized personal property.

title: State v. Wilson
description: Whether Hawaiʻi's laws restricting the public carry of firearms and ammunition (HRS § 134-25(a) and § 134-27(a)) violate an individual's right to bear arms under the Hawaiʻi Constitution and the Second Amendment to the United States Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Christopher Wilson lacked standing to challenge the licensing law (HRS § 134-9) because he did not apply for a license, and that Hawaiʻi's firearm regulations are constitutional and do not violate any right to carry firearms in public.
defendant_argument: Christopher Wilson argued that Hawaiʻi's 'place to keep' laws (HRS § 134-25(a) and § 134-27(a)) infringe upon his constitutional right to carry a handgun for self-defense outside the home, as established by the Second Amendment and Article I, Section 17 of the Hawaiʻi Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the circuit court's order dismissing the charges against Christopher Wilson, holding that there is no state constitutional right to carry a firearm in public in Hawaiʻi and that the challenged laws do not violate Wilson's rights under either the Hawaiʻi or United States Constitutions.

title: State v. Lafoga
description: Whether the circuit court's decision to empanel an anonymous jury, without strong justification and without taking precautions to mitigate prejudice, violated the defendants' constitutional rights to a fair trial, presumption of innocence, impartial jury, and effective assistance of counsel.
plaintiff_argument: The State implicitly argued that the anonymous jury was permissible or that any error in empaneling it was harmless, and that the court took reasonable precautions.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the anonymous jury violated their constitutional rights to presumption of innocence, an impartial jury, effective assistance of counsel, and an impartial tribunal, constituting structural error requiring a new trial.
decision_outcome: The court upheld the circuit court's decision to empanel an anonymous jury, concluding that any error was harmless.

title: State v. Hewitt
description: Whether Cyrina L. Hewitt was in custody for Miranda purposes while being questioned by police in a hospital bed, thereby requiring Miranda warnings before her statements could be used as evidence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Hewitt was not in custody at the time of questioning, and therefore, Miranda warnings were not required.
defendant_argument: Hewitt argued that she was subjected to custodial interrogation without the requisite Miranda warnings because she was in custody, even before probable cause developed, due to her medical condition and the circumstances of the police questioning.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Hawaii reversed the Intermediate Court of Appeals' judgment that ordered a remand and affirmed the district court's judgment of nolle prosequi for both counts against Hewitt, effectively dismissing her convictions.

title: Ohana v. Univiversity of Hawai'i
description: Whether the burden of proof shifts to the government defendant in constitutional challenges to administrative rules based on a violation of Article XII, Section 7 of the Hawai'i Constitution, and what standard governs such challenges.
plaintiff_argument: The burden of proof should shift to the government defendant to prove the rules are reasonable and do not unduly limit constitutional rights.
defendant_argument: The burden of proof remains with the challenging party, and the Salerno 'no set of circumstances' test should apply to constitutional challenges.
decision_outcome: The court held that the burden of proof does not shift to the government defendant but remains with the challenging party. It also held that the Ka Pa'akai framework applies to administrative rulemaking, requiring agencies to conduct a contemporaneous analysis of Native Hawaiian traditional and customary rights before adopting rules, and setting a three-part test for plaintiffs to challenge such rules.

title: State v. Canosa
description: Whether a sixteen-month delay in sentencing deprived the defendant of due process and the opportunity for allocution, especially when the delay precluded sentencing prior to the expiration of the ordinary maximum term.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the delay in sentencing did not prevent the court from legally resentencing the defendant to extended terms, and that the court retained jurisdiction to do so.
defendant_argument: Canosa argued that the sixteen-month delay in sentencing violated his due process rights and right to allocution, and that extended terms could not be imposed because the ordinary maximum terms had already expired due to the State's unreasonable delay.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the Intermediate Court of Appeals' judgment, ordered the defendant's immediate release from State custody, and remanded the case to the circuit court to reflect time served nunc pro tunc from the date of release.

title: State v. Obrero
description: Whether Hawaiʻi Revised Statutes (HRS) § 801-1, which requires a grand jury indictment for felony prosecutions, was implicitly repealed or superseded by a 1982 constitutional amendment allowing felony charges via preliminary hearing.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the 1982 constitutional amendment to Article I, Section 10, effectively nullified HRS § 801-1's grand jury protections by authorizing the State to use complaints and preliminary hearings to initiate felony prosecutions, and that HRS § 801-1 was implicitly repealed.
defendant_argument: Obrero argued that HRS § 801-1 plainly requires a grand jury indictment for felony prosecutions not within district court jurisdiction or chargeable by information, that the statute has not been implicitly repealed, and that the State's use of a preliminary hearing after a grand jury no-bill is unconstitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's denial of Obrero's motion to dismiss, ruling that the State cannot subject Obrero to trial and sentencing without a grand jury indictment as required by HRS § 801-1.

title: State v. Sagapolutele-Silva
description: Whether the existence of probable cause alone is sufficient to establish that a suspect is in custody for Miranda purposes, or if a totality-of-the-circumstances approach should be used.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that the "totality of the circumstances" approach should be used to determine custody for Miranda warnings, and that probable cause alone is not dispositive. They contend Sagapolutele-Silva was not in custody during the traffic stop or SFST.
defendant_argument: Sagapolutele-Silva agrees that the "totality of the circumstances" approach should be used, but argues that she was in custody during the OVUII investigation, requiring Miranda warnings earlier.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the district court's order suppressing Sagapolutele-Silva's statements and the ICA's judgment, clarifying that the totality-of-the-circumstances test applies and Sagapolutele-Silva was not in custody until after the SFST.

title: Hicks v. 2021 Hawaii Reapportionment Commission
description: Whether the 2021 Hawaiʻi Reapportionment Commission was required to fully implement the 'district within district' guidelines for legislative districts, or if it had discretion to consider them alongside other policy objectives.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that the 2021 Reapportionment Plan is invalid because it fails to give adequate effect to constitutional and statutory 'district within district' guidelines, which require representative districts to be wholly included within senatorial districts and legislative districts within U.S. congressional districts, even when practicable.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that it satisfied its obligations by considering the 'district within district' guidelines alongside other policy objectives and that the guidelines are discretionary, not mandatory, thus the Plan is valid and no abuse of discretion occurred.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitioners' request, ruling that the Reapportionment Commission has discretion in applying 'district within district' guidelines and is not required to give them any particular effect, as long as they are considered.

title: League of Women Voters of Honolulu  v. State
description: Whether a bill that has been substantially amended with non-germane content must undergo three new readings in each legislative house to comply with the Hawai'i Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The bill (Act 84) did not receive the required three readings in each house after a non-germane amendment changed its purpose, thus violating Article III, Section 15 of the Hawai'i Constitution.
defendant_argument: The Legislature's own rules of procedure permit a bill to be read only by number and title and do not require new readings after an amendment, even if the contents are entirely substituted, and the process followed these rules.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the circuit court's judgment, ruling that Act 84 was unconstitutionally enacted because it did not receive the required three readings after a non-germane amendment, and remanded the case with instructions to grant the plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment.

title: In re Individuals in Custody of the State
description: Whether the Supreme Court of Hawaii should grant extraordinary relief to order the expedited release of certain inmates and mandate specific public health measures in correctional facilities during the COVID-19 pandemic, or if existing legal mechanisms and changed circumstances render such relief unnecessary.
plaintiff_argument: The Office of the Public Defender (OPD) argued that the COVID-19 pandemic created an unprecedented public health emergency requiring extraordinary relief, including the expedited release of certain categories of inmates and court-ordered public health measures in correctional facilities, to protect inmates and the public.
defendant_argument: The respondents (DPS, prosecuting attorneys) argued that conditions had changed since prior petitions, with widespread vaccine availability and a federal settlement addressing pandemic response in correctional facilities, making the requested extraordinary relief unwarranted and that existing legal mechanisms for inmate release were sufficient.
decision_outcome: The court granted the petition in part, ordering the Department of Public Safety (DPS) to comply with HRS § 353-6.2 regarding periodic reviews and transmission of findings for pretrial detainees, but denied all other requests for extraordinary relief.

title: State v. Lee
description: Whether evidence obtained after police entered Joshua Lee's bedroom without a warrant should be suppressed, with Lee arguing it should be suppressed due to an unlawful search and the State arguing it should not be suppressed due to an emergency aid exception or because Lee's subsequent actions were new crimes.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the evidence should not be suppressed because an emergency aid exception applied, or alternatively, Lee's actions constituted a new crime, and the evidence was not "fruit of the poisonous tree."
defendant_argument: Lee argued that the ICA erred in vacating the suppression order, contending that the State failed to establish exigent circumstances to justify the warrantless search, which was inconsistent with the Hawai'i Constitution's enhanced protections.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the ICA's judgment, which vacated the circuit court's order to suppress evidence, but on different grounds, meaning the evidence will not be suppressed.
